cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: The age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales is 10 — one of the lowest in Europe. In Scotland it was raised to 12 in 2021 (from 8). Many argue it should be raised to 14.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: Children aged 10-17 are dealt with in youth courts, not adult courts. Youth courts are less formal: no public gallery, judges don't wear wigs, parents must attend, and reporting restrictions protect the young person's identity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: Young offenders can receive: Referral Orders (first offence, attend a youth offender panel), Youth Rehabilitation Orders (community sentence with requirements), or Detention and Training Orders (custodial, from age 12).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: ASSET assessments identify the needs of young offenders and the factors contributing to their offending behaviour — such as family problems, education, substance misuse, and mental health.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: At 16: can work full-time, join the armed forces with parental consent, consent to medical treatment, and marry with parental consent.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: At 17: can drive a car (with a provisional licence), and can be remanded to a Young Offender Institution.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: At 18: full adult legal rights and responsibilities apply — can vote, serve on a jury, buy alcohol, and be tried in an adult court.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: Stop and search disproportionately affects young people from ethnic minority backgrounds — Black people are around 7 times more likely to be stopped than white people.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: Schools have legal duties regarding bullying, exclusion, safeguarding, and the wellbeing of students. The Children Act 1989 and 2004 set out these responsibilities.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: Anti-social behaviour impacts young people both as perpetrators and victims. Young people are often perceived as causing ASB but are also frequently victims of it.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: Youth offending teams (YOTs) are multi-agency teams that work with young offenders to address the causes of offending and prevent reoffending.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Young People & the Law
cards.back: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) sets out children's rights, though the UK has not fully incorporated it into domestic law.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — young people & the law?
cards.back: 1. For Young People & the Law questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Young People & the Law to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
